analysis.one_liner: Cuts off federal student aid to for-profit colleges and tightens rules on nonprofit conversions.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate education committee on October 17, 2019, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make for-profit colleges ineligible for federal student aid, ending the flow of federal grants and loans to schools run as profit-making businesses. It would also disqualify any school whose institution or executives filed for bankruptcy, committed fraud or misrepresentation involving federal student aid, or whose executives previously worked at a college that closed while taking federal aid. And it would set conditions on for-profit schools converting to nonprofit status, requiring public review and independent valuation so owners cannot quietly keep control or profit from the switch.
analysis.who_benefits: Students who attend for-profit colleges and borrow federal loans, and taxpayers who fund those loans. For-profit schools have historically produced above-average loan defaults and well-documented cases of misrepresentation; cutting off federal aid and screening conversions to nonprofit status would shift that risk off students and taxpayers. The bill also includes a one-year grace period so students can finish the academic year at a school that loses eligibility.
analysis.who_benefits_short: For-profit college students and federal taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Makes for-profit colleges ineligible for federal student aid, removing the federal grants and loans that are their main revenue source [S2][S3].

Disqualifies schools from federal aid if the institution filed for bankruptcy, its owners or executives were convicted of or settled fraud involving federal student aid, or its executives previously worked at an aid-receiving school that closed [S2][S3].

Requires that a for-profit school converting to nonprofit status pay fair value for acquired assets, sever outside economic benefits to board members and former owners, and publish the application in the Federal Register for public comment before approval [S2][S3].
Caps distance-education enrollment at half the student body and incarcerated students at a quarter, and requires certificate programs to prepare students for gainful employment [S3].
Lets students already enrolled keep receiving loans for the academic year after a school loses eligibility, so they are not left stranded mid-year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit college companies and their owners and investors, whose access to roughly the entire federal student-aid pipeline would end. Schools that misused aid, or whose founders wanted to convert to nonprofit status while retaining control, would lose the ability to do so. Some nontraditional students, including working adults who chose for-profit schools for flexible schedules, would need to find public or nonprofit alternatives.

drawbacks.text: An outright cutoff is blunt: many for-profit schools enroll working adults, career changers, and students without traditional credentials, and the bill relies on public and nonprofit institutions absorbing that demand, which it does not build out [S2].

The executive disqualification is broad — a school loses eligibility if any executive ever worked at an aid-receiving college that later closed — which could sweep in schools and staff with no record of wrongdoing [S3].

Existing students at affected schools would face disruption after the one-year grace period, and honest for-profit operators would lose a business model entirely rather than facing graduated penalties [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but lopsided in the bill's favor: for-profit schools have repeatedly been the site of federal-aid fraud, high defaults, and aggressive marketing to low-income students, and the bill protects current students from abrupt loss of aid with a transition year. The cost falls on a specific industry and on students who would have to find other schools. The honest weakness is that the bill cuts supply without building alternatives for the nontraditional students those schools serve.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee took no action on it before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown, joined by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, introduced the bill in the Senate on October 17, 2019 [S1][S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S5][S1].
The bill would have made for-profit colleges ineligible for federal student aid and barred schools tied to bankruptcy or student-aid fraud [S2].
It would also have imposed conditions and public comment on conversions from for-profit to nonprofit status, targeting arrangements where former owners keep control or economic benefit [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit college companies, which kept unrestricted access to federal student aid dollars, and their owners, who retained the ability to convert to nonprofit status without the bill's independent valuation and public-comment safeguards.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit colleges kept federal aid dollars

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic sponsorship — one sponsor and one cosponsor — and died in a committee chaired by a Republican without any recorded vote, so no roll call shows where parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would cut off federal student aid — the industry's dominant revenue source — and bar schools tied to bankruptcy or aid fraud from getting it back. These schools' revenue comes from federal loans and grants taken on by students, many of whom end up with debt and weak job prospects, so the industry's interest in this bill runs against the students it enrolls.

industries.industry: For-profit college owners seeking nonprofit conversions
industries.note: The bill would require independent valuation of assets, public comment on conversion applications, and a ban on economic benefits to former owners or board members, closing the route by which for-profit companies rebrand as nonprofits while former owners keep control or service contracts.

With for-profit schools cut off from federal aid, students seeking credentials would be steered toward public and nonprofit institutions, which the bill treats as the legitimate channel for federal student aid.
